passage: Damini, before you judge me, let me explain. Last March, every single guy on my hostel floor was talking about this new digital coin. Group chat, mess, even the laundry line. Forty people. Forty! I thought: forty engineering students can't all be wrong, right? I didn't read anything about it. I didn't know who made it. I just saw the number of people and the green arrows on their phones, and I put in my whole semester's pocket money. I'm Tanvir, and I once lectured you about reading terms and conditions. Anyway. It dropped to almost nothing in April. The funny thing? When I asked around, most of the forty had joined because the others had. Nobody had actually checked anything.

qa.q: How many people on Tanvir's floor were talking about the coin?
qa.a: Forty people.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir feel safe putting in the whole semester's pocket money?
qa.a: Tanvir thought forty engineering students couldn't all be wrong, so the crowd itself felt like proof.

qa.q: What would you advise Tanvir the next time something is suddenly popular?
qa.a: Find out who made it and what it actually is, and talk it over with a trusted adult before putting in money, however many have joined.

qa.q: What might Damini be thinking while listening to this?
qa.a: Damini might find it ironic, since Tanvir once lectured Damini about reading terms and conditions.

grounding: A student puts a semester's pocket money into a coin because forty hostel-mates had, treating popularity as proof.

passage: I'm Tenzin, Binita's roommate, and I watched her decide how to vote in the student council election. Two weeks before, she had a list on her desk: hostel water, library hours, the women's safety committee. She'd even read both manifestos. Then, three days before polling, the whole corridor started wearing Rakesh's yellow badges. Posters on every door. In the mess, people just said, "Everyone's voting Rakesh." Binita came back one evening with a yellow badge. When I asked what his plan for the library was, she said, "Honestly, no idea. But half the campus can't be wrong." Her list was still on the desk, and his name wasn't on it. I don't know exactly why she changed. Maybe she just didn't want to be on the losing side.

qa.q: What colour were Rakesh's badges?
qa.a: They were yellow.

qa.q: What does Binita's 'half the campus can't be wrong' suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she was treating the number of supporters as proof, even though she didn't know his plan for the library.

qa.q: What could Binita do before polling day?
qa.a: She could check Rakesh's plans against her own list about water, library hours and safety, then vote for whoever matches it best.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Binita's change?
qa.a: Tenzin notices the list still on the desk and wonders whether Binita just didn't want to be on the losing side.

grounding: A roommate watches a student drop her own checklist and vote for the popular candidate because everyone else is.

passage:
Monday. In the college canteen, it seemed everyone had joined the new home business group selling skincare kits. Usha's feed was full of classmates posing with boxes. "Two hundred students already," Imran said. "Can't all be fools." Usha paid the joining fee that night without reading the terms.
Thursday. The group's leader messaged: the way to earn was to bring in five friends, each paying the same fee. Usha asked what happened if the friends didn't sell anything. The leader replied with a video of people clapping.
The following Wednesday. Usha sat on the hostel bed with three unopened kits and a list of friends Usha didn't want to ask. Imran came by. "I haven't recruited anyone either," he admitted. "I don't think most of the two hundred have." Usha opened the terms and read them for the first time.

qa.q: What was the way to earn, according to the group's leader?
qa.a: The way to earn was to bring in five friends, each paying the same fee.

qa.q: Why did Usha pay without reading the terms?
qa.a: Usha felt reassured by the crowd: with two hundred students already in and Imran saying they can't all be fools, the popularity felt like enough proof.

qa.q: What could Usha and Imran do now?
qa.a: They could stop recruiting, read the terms together, and ask a trusted adult or the college for guidance about the fee.

qa.q: How might the friends on Usha's list feel if Usha had pushed them to join?
qa.a: They might feel pressured and used, paying a fee mainly so Usha could earn, which could strain the friendships.

grounding: A student joins a selling scheme because two hundred classmates had, and only later reads what it really is.

passage:
Nandini, you're about to join that study-abroad agency because all your friends did? Sit with your Farida Phuphi for a minute.
In 1996 I was twenty, a small-town girl in my second year of college in Hyderabad. Everybody in my hostel was signing up with one agency for a nursing course abroad. The queue went round the building. I thought, if two hundred girls are joining, it must be good. So many people can't be wrong. I didn't ask which university, or whether the course was recognised. I paid my registration fee from my scholarship money.
Months later we learned the college on the brochure didn't exist the way they described. A few girls lost everything. I lost my fee, and my Abba's trust for a while.
The crowd felt like proof. It wasn't. It was just a crowd.

qa.q: How many girls did Farida think were joining the agency?
qa.a: She thought two hundred girls were joining.

qa.q: Why did joining feel safe to young Farida?
qa.a: The long queue and all her hostel friends signing up made her feel that so many people couldn't be wrong, so she didn't check the university or the course.

qa.q: What could Nandini check before joining the agency her friends chose?
qa.a: Nandini could ask which university it is, whether the course is recognised, and check with a trusted adult or the college itself, instead of treating the number of friends as proof.

qa.q: How might Farida's Abba have felt when the fee was lost?
qa.a: Her Abba likely felt hurt and worried, which is why Farida says she lost his trust for a while, not just the money.

grounding: An elder recalls joining a popular agency because everyone in her hostel did, treating popularity as evidence, and losing her fee.

passage:
The registration link for the "Global Leaders Certificate" closed at 6 p.m., and it was 5:40 when Lalremsiami, twenty, finally saw it. Her class group had exploded: three hundred students from her college had signed up. Screenshots of payment receipts kept popping up.
"Three hundred people," she told Shalini, grabbing her phone on the bus. "They can't all be wrong."
"What does it actually give you?" Shalini asked.
"Leadership sessions. A certificate. It's… I don't know exactly. But everyone's in."
"Who runs it? Is it from the college?"
Lalremsiami scrolled. The page had lots of photos of smiling students and very little else. The bus jolted; the signal dropped. 5:52.
"I'll just pay and check later," she said, thumb over the button. "If three hundred of us are wrong, at least we're wrong together."
Shalini gently put her hand over the screen. "Or you wait eight minutes and ask the college office tomorrow."

qa.q: How many students from her college had signed up for the certificate?
qa.a: Three hundred students from her college had signed up.

qa.q: Why did paying without checking feel reasonable to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt rushed and afraid of being left out, with the deadline minutes away and hundreds of classmates posting receipts, so the crowd itself felt like proof the certificate was worth it.

qa.q: What choice did Shalini put in front of Lalremsiami at the last minute?
qa.a: Shalini suggested letting the deadline pass and asking the college office tomorrow, so the decision would rest on facts about who runs it, not on how many had joined.

qa.q: What would change if the link had no signup counter or receipts in the group?
qa.a: Without the crowd, Lalremsiami would likely notice the page has little information and ask what it gives before paying.

grounding: It shows a young adult ready to pay for a programme because hundreds of peers joined, treating popularity as evidence under time pressure.

passage: Ishita, you say you'll join because everyone in the hostel already has? Let your Madhuri maasi tell you about the year I was nineteen, in a hostel in Nagpur. Suddenly every girl on our floor was selling soaps and creams for some company. They paid to join and then got others to join. There were meetings with music and a man in a shiny suit. Forty girls, then sixty. I thought, sixty people can't all be wrong, and I gave my whole scholarship to join. Six months later the office was locked and the man was gone. Sixty of us had been wrong together. Your nana didn't shout. He just asked, "Did you check what they actually sold, or only how many were buying?" I've asked that question about everything since.

qa.q: Why did young Madhuri believe the scheme was safe?
qa.a: She felt reassured and excited because sixty girls had joined, so the crowd felt like proof it was genuine.

qa.q: What question from the story could have changed the choice, and why?
qa.a: "Did you check what they actually sold, or only how many were buying?" It points to real evidence instead of the crowd.

qa.q: How might Madhuri's father have felt when the office was locked?
qa.a: He was probably worried and sad for her, yet chose to ask a gentle question rather than shout.

grounding: An aunt recalls joining a scheme at nineteen because sixty hostel mates had, treating popularity as proof, and losing her scholarship.

passage: Voting in the student union election closed at four, and it was 3:50 when Anirban ran into the hall, out of breath. "Who are you voting for?" asked Rajni, standing in the queue. "Pritam, obviously. Everyone's voting Pritam. His posters are everywhere, and he's got the most followers." "What's he promising?" Anirban opened his mouth. "Something about the canteen? I don't know. But five hundred people can't be wrong." "Five hundred people might all have the same reason as you," Rajni said. The queue moved. Anirban took out his phone and, with seven minutes left, opened the two manifestos for the first time. Pritam's was one page of slogans. The other candidate's had a plan for the short library hours he complained about every week. At 3:58 he stood in the booth, pen hovering.

passage: In the Koramangala office canteen, everyone was talking about the same thing: a new coin on a trading app that had "gone up four times in a month." Dolma, three months into her first job, listened to five colleagues describe their profits. By evening she had the app open and her savings ready to move. "If everyone's in, it can't be a scam," she told her flatmate Chetan. Chetan looked over. "What does the coin actually do?" Dolma scrolled. "It... has a community?" "And how many people lost money on the last three coins everyone was talking about?" She didn't know. She closed the app, a little annoyed, and called her cousin, who worked as a financial adviser. "Don't decide tonight," the cousin said. "Let's go through it on Sunday."

qa.q: What did colleagues say the coin had done?
qa.a: Gone up four times in a month.

qa.q: Why did Dolma think the coin couldn't be a scam?
qa.a: She felt reassured and excited because so many colleagues were in, so popularity felt like evidence that it was safe.

qa.q: What did Dolma do before moving her savings, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She closed the app and called her cousin, a financial adviser, to go through it on Sunday, instead of following the crowd that night.

qa.q: How does Chetan see the coin?
qa.a: Chetan is doubtful, wanting to know what the coin actually does and what happened with past popular coins.

grounding: A young woman nearly follows colleagues into a popular coin, treating popularity as proof, until a question and a qualified adviser slow her down.

passage: In my second year of college in Nashik, I joined the "business opportunity" because all eleven boys on my hostel floor had joined. I'm Jatin, and I'm usually careful, but that week I wasn't. The meetings were full of cheering, and everyone I knew was there. If so many smart people were in, how could it be a trick? My cousin Salma didi asked me on the phone, "Bhai, what do they actually sell?" I didn't really know. "Everyone's making money," I said, which wasn't true either. I paid the joining fee from my scholarship money. Three months later the organisers stopped answering calls. The eleven of us sat in one room, staring at each other. We had all joined because the others had. Now I ask my father or a teacher I trust before I sign anything, however many friends are already in.

qa.a: All eleven boys on my hostel floor had joined.

qa.q: What does Jatin do now, and why is it a good habit?
qa.a: Jatin asks his father or a trusted teacher before signing anything, however many friends are already in, so popularity doesn't replace real checking.

passage:
Counsellor's note, second-year electives, 3 July.
Lalit came to finalise his elective today. He had chosen Financial Markets. When I asked why, he said, "Everyone's taking it. Ninety students signed up in the first hour." I asked what he enjoyed most last year. Without a pause: the psychology module and the field survey. He hadn't looked at the Behavioural Research elective at all.
His friend Payal was waiting outside with the same form, the same choice.
I didn't tell him what to pick. I asked him to read both course outlines and tell me, on Friday, which one he would choose if nobody in his batch would ever know. He laughed, a bit embarrassed, and said, "That's a scary question." He took both outlines.
Follow-up: Friday, 11 a.m.

qa.q: How many students signed up for Financial Markets in the first hour?
qa.a: Ninety students signed up in the first hour.

qa.q: What does Lalit's "That's a scary question" suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He seemed embarrassed and uneasy, sensing he had picked the elective because of the crowd, not his own interest.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Lalit, and why might it work?
qa.a: By asking him to read both outlines and choose as if nobody would know, so his own interest could count more than the crowd.

qa.q: How might Payal's choice be affected if Lalit changes his elective?
qa.a: Payal might start questioning her own reasons too, since she seemed to be following the same crowd.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a student choosing a course because it is popular, assuming ninety people can't be wrong.

passage:
Wednesday

Joined the Entrepreneurship Cell today. Everyone's joining it. It had the longest queue at the club fair, like two hundred people. I figured if that many people want it, it must be the best club.

I didn't even stop at the music society's stall. That's the one I actually wanted. I've played guitar since I was twelve.

But Vaibhav said, "E-Cell is where everyone is. That's where the networking happens." And the queue was so long it felt like proof.

Now I'm lying here thinking. Two hundred people joining something doesn't mean it's right for me. It just means it's popular. And maybe half of them joined for the same reason I did: because the queue was long.

The music society had fifteen people. Fifteen people who actually love music.

Going back tomorrow to sign up there too. Maybe instead.

Nilesh

qa.q: How many people were in the E-Cell queue?
qa.a: Like two hundred people.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh join the E-Cell without much thought?
qa.a: Nilesh felt reassured by the long queue, treating popularity as proof it was the best club, and didn't want to miss out.

qa.q: What did Nilesh realise, and what is the next step?
qa.a: Nilesh realised popularity isn't evidence of fit, and plans to sign up for the music society, which matches a real interest.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Nilesh's change?
qa.a: Vaibhav might be surprised, since Vaibhav valued networking, but could respect Nilesh following a real interest.

grounding: A young adult joins a college club mainly because it is the most popular, treating the crowd as evidence.

passage:
That June, every farmer in Jatin's village near Latur was sowing soybean. The seed shop had a queue down the road. Jatin, twenty-one and newly in charge of his father's fields, joined the queue too.

"Why soybean?" asked his sister Irawati, walking with him.

"Everyone's doing it."

"Last year you said the lower field floods. Soybean hates standing water."

"But the whole village can't be wrong."

"The whole village doesn't farm that field," Irawati said.

Jatin stopped. He had been so sure. Every neighbour, every uncle, every chat at the tea stall said soybean. It had felt like evidence.

But none of them had looked at his lower field.

He stepped out of the queue. "I'll ask the agriculture officer about the lower field first," he said. "Maybe soybean for the top field, something else below."

Irawati smiled. "Now you're farming, not following."

qa.q: What crop was every farmer sowing?
qa.a: Soybean.

qa.q: Why was Jatin going to sow soybean on all his fields?
qa.a: Jatin felt reassured because the whole village was doing it, and popularity felt like proof it was right.

qa.q: What did Jatin decide after Irawati's question, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Jatin decided to ask the agriculture officer about the lower field first, judging his own land rather than following the crowd.

qa.q: How does Irawati seem to see Jatin's final decision?
qa.a: Irawati seems pleased and proud, saying he's now farming rather than following.

grounding: A young farmer nearly sows the same crop as the whole village, assuming so many people can't be wrong.

passage: By the second week of December, the student union election had taken over the Leeds campus. Everywhere Nkechi looked, people wore the same orange badge for Callum, the candidate with the catchy slogan. "Three thousand likes on his video," Liam said, pinning one to his scarf. "They can't all be wrong." Nkechi hadn't read a single manifesto. On the way to the library she passed Callum's stall, giant orange balloons bobbing in the wind and a queue for free hot chocolate. At the voting booth she hesitated, pen above the paper. She knew nothing about the other two names. Orange badges filled the corridor behind her. She ticked Callum. It felt like joining a warm crowd on a cold day. Later, in the library, she finally opened his manifesto. It was mostly the slogan, repeated.
